ruleIntents.intent: Checks that any element carrying an EXPLICIT ARIA role attribute also declares every WAI-ARIA "required state/property" for that role, with a non-empty value — unless WAI-ARIA defines an implicit default for that property (e.g. aria-selected defaults to false on option), or the property only becomes required under a condition that isn't met (e.g. separator only requires aria-valuenow when focusable). It is a purely structural DOM check: it reads the explicit role token, looks up that role's required-properties list in the ARIA spec, and verifies the attributes are present and non-empty. It does NOT evaluate whether the values are correct, whether the widget behaves, or whether a native fallback would actually be announced.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 1.3.1 "information, structure, and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined." Specifically the programmatic-determinability of a custom-component's STATE/PROPERTY relationships: when an author overrides native semantics with role=, the role's required ARIA states/properties are the mechanism by which the component's structural info (heading level, checked state, expanded/collapsed, value position, controls relationship) is exposed to the a11y tree. The rule guards the "required states and properties are set so the relationship is programmatically determinable" limb — not naming, not headings-as-structure, not table/list/form-label relationships. Note the spec itself flags 1.3.1 as only a SECONDARY/less-strict requirement: the rule is primarily an ARIA 1.2 5.2.2 author-conformance check, and AT fallback to non-standard defaults means some failed examples can still pass 1.3.1.
ruleIntents.applicability: Any HTML or SVG element that (a) is included in the accessibility tree AND (b) has an explicit semantic role, EXCEPT when that explicit role is identical to the element's implicit role (e.g. input type=checkbox role=checkbox — the native attribute then satisfies the requirement). Elements with no role, or roles hidden from the a11y tree (display:none / aria-hidden), are inapplicable.
ruleIntents.expectation: For each in-scope target, every WAI-ARIA required state and property for its role is present and not the empty string "", UNLESS the property has a WAI-ARIA implicit/default value for that role (then omission is allowed), or the property is only conditionally required and the condition is absent. Failing = a required property is missing or empty; passing = all required (and currently-required) properties are explicitly set.

FAIL: required state missing where pre-ARIA-1.2 default no longer applies (role=switch / role=checkbox without aria-checked)
FAIL: conditionally-required property missing because condition now met (role=separator + tabindex=0 -> focusable widget -> aria-valuenow required)
FAIL: composite widget missing a required property (role=combobox without aria-expanded)

INAPPLICABLE: explicit role identical to implicit role (input checkbox role=checkbox)

syntheticNarrowness: Every fixture is a bare static HTML snippet with one isolated target, a <title>, and at most a sibling label/main — no surrounding page chrome, CSS framework, or real layout; real components live inside nested DOM where role inheritance, presentational-role conflicts, and required-owned-element relationships (e.g. listbox->option) interact.

Only a handful of roles are exercised (heading, checkbox, switch, scrollbar, option, separator, combobox). Many roles with required props are untested: spinbutton/slider (aria-valuenow), radio/menuitemradio/menuitemcheckbox (aria-checked), tab (aria-selected default), the whole grid/treegrid family, etc.

All values are present-or-absent. Empty-string failures (aria-level=""), whitespace-only values, and invalid-but-present values are described in the expectation but NOT represented by any fixture — the disk corpus only tests presence vs total omission.

ARIA values are never wrong or contradictory: the rule deliberately ignores value correctness, but the fixtures also never include the realistic case of a present-but-bogus value (aria-checked="yes", aria-valuenow="abc"), which a human reviewing 1.3.1 would still flag.

Hidden-from-tree is tested with a single mechanism (style=display:none); aria-hidden=true, visibility:hidden, off-screen positioning, hidden attribute, and detached/not-yet-rendered nodes are all unrepresented despite being the common real-world reasons a component is excluded from the tree.

The implicit-role exception is tested with exactly one element (input checkbox role=checkbox); the broader redundant-role landscape (nav role=navigation, button role=button, ul role=list, a href role=link) and the harder case of role overriding native semantics with conflicting required attrs is missing.

Conditional requirement is shown only via separator+focusability through tabindex; other conditional triggers (focusability via contenteditable, native focusable elements, or role-context-dependent requirements) aren't covered.

No dynamic/state-change scenarios: required states like aria-expanded, aria-checked, aria-selected are inherently runtime-mutable, but fixtures are static snapshots — they never capture the real failure mode where the attribute exists at load but is never updated as the widget toggles.

Components are decontextualized: a combobox/listbox pair, a scrollbar with its controlled main, etc. appear in isolation, so the relationship-integrity dimension of 1.3.1 (does aria-controls actually point at a real, meaningful target; is the owned-element structure complete) is reduced to mere attribute presence, not semantic validity.

Only HTML targets are present on disk; the rule's applicability explicitly includes SVG elements with explicit roles, but no SVG fixture exists, so SVG-specific tree-inclusion and role behavior are untested.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every WAI-ARIA state/property attribute placed on an element is one that is ALLOWED on that element — i.e., it is either (a) a global ARIA state/property (allowed everywhere), (b) an inherited/supported/required state/property of the element's semantic role, or (c) explicitly permitted on that HTML element per "ARIA in HTML". It does NOT check the attribute's VALUE (whether the value is valid/meaningful), nor whether the attribute is actually relevant/needed — purely whether the attribute is permitted to appear there at all. The failure mode it targets is authors attaching ARIA attributes that the role/element does not support (e.g. aria-sort on a button), which browsers/AT silently ignore, so intended state information never reaches AT users.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "relationships/programmatically-determinable information" limb of 1.3.1: ARIA states/properties are the programmatic mechanism by which an element's role-related information and state are conveyed to assistive technology. This rule exercises it only obliquely — it catches ARIA attributes that are SILENTLY DROPPED because they are not permitted on the element/role, so any info those attributes were meant to expose is lost from the accessibility tree. Note the rule's own mapping marks 1.3.1 (and 4.1.2) as SECONDARY requirements: 1.3.1 is "less strict" than the rule because the rule fails irrelevant-but-permitted-elsewhere ARIA that 1.3.1 may still consider passing. The rule's primary normative anchors are the ARIA 1.2 author requirement (8.6 State and Property Attribute Processing) and technique ARIA5, not an SC directly.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any WAI-ARIA state or property (an aria-* attribute that is a state or property) specified on an HTML or SVG element that is included in the accessibility tree. Scope notes that constrain it: (1) only states/properties, role itself is out of scope; (2) the element must be in the accessibility tree — elements removed via display:none / aria-hidden / not rendered are inapplicable (Inapplicable Example 2); (3) an element with no aria-* state/property attribute at all is inapplicable (Inapplicable Example 1); (4) the EFFECTIVE semantic role is what matters, including Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution (role=none on a focusable button still resolves to button — Passed Example 10) and host-language allowances independent of role (input type=password allows aria-required — Passed Example 11).
ruleIntents.expectation: For each ARIA state/property target, at least ONE of three must hold: (1) GLOBAL — it is a global ARIA state/property (e.g. aria-busy, aria-label), permitted on any element regardless of role; OR (2) SEMANTIC ROLE — it is an inherited, supported, or required state/property of the element's effective semantic role (explicit role= or implicit role), e.g. aria-pressed on button, aria-checked required by checkbox, aria-required inherited by switch from its checkbox superclass; OR (3) LANGUAGE FEATURE — the element is HTML and the attribute is allowed on that specific element per ARIA in HTML even absent a matching role (e.g. aria-required on input type=password). Attributes with value "undefined" or empty are still evaluated for permittedness (value validity is explicitly out of scope). If none of the three hold (e.g. aria-sort on button, aria-orientation on audio), it FAILS.

Value-validity is explicitly excluded, so cases like aria-checked on a checkbox with a nonsense value, or aria-controls pointing to a missing id, fall outside — masking real info/relationship breakage that 1.3.1 actually cares about
SVG coverage is a single graphics-object with a global property; supported/required props of specific graphics roles and the broader SVG/ARIA surface are untested
No negative interaction with sibling/required-context constraints (e.g. aria-posinset/aria-setsize outside a set, aria-level outside heading/treeitem) which are common real authoring mistakes
Single-language, single-attribute pages give no signal on pages with dozens of mixed valid/invalid ARIA attributes where the FP/FN behavior under noise matters

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every non-empty, non-whitespace-only `role` attribute on a visible HTML/SVG element contains at least one token that is a valid, non-abstract WAI-ARIA role (including Graphics-ARIA and DPUB-ARIA roles, and accounting for the space-separated fallback-role token list). It is purely a syntactic/vocabulary validation of the role token string — catching typos like role="lnik" or made-up roles like role="bibliographic-reference" — not a check of whether the chosen role is semantically correct, appropriate for the element, or matches the content's actual meaning.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "programmatically determined" / "presented through markup" limb of 1.3.1 — specifically the relationship/role information that is conveyed via ARIA markup. It exercises the integrity of the role-conveying mechanism (a valid ARIA role can expose semantics to AT), but only at the level of "is this token a real role keyword," not "does the role correctly describe the relationship/structure." Note the rule's own mapping calls 1.3.1 a SECONDARY/less-strict requirement: an invalid explicit role falls back to the element's implicit role, which may still satisfy 1.3.1, so a failure of this rule is not necessarily a failure of 1.3.1.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any `role` attribute where BOTH: (a) the attribute value is neither empty ("") nor only ASCII whitespace (i.e., contains at least one token); AND (b) the attribute is on an HTML or SVG element that is not programmatically hidden. Excludes: elements with no role attribute, role with no value (role), role="", whitespace-only role values, and roles on programmatically hidden elements (e.g., aria-hidden="true" or display:none — note CSS Styling is a required input aspect for the hidden determination).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each applicable role attribute has at least one space-separated token that is a valid value corresponding to a non-abstract role from the WAI-ARIA specifications (core ARIA, Graphics-ARIA, DPUB-ARIA). Because of fallback-role semantics, only ONE token in the list needs to be valid for the target to pass; the presence of additional invalid tokens (e.g., role="searchfield searchbox") does not cause failure.

syntheticNarrowness: Tiny single-element fixtures: each example is one element in isolation, with no surrounding DOM structure, ancestor roles, or required owned/parent role contexts (e.g., listitem without list, option without listbox) that real pages exhibit.

Tests only token-vocabulary validity, never semantic appropriateness — the dominant real-world 1.3.1 failure (a valid-but-wrong role, e.g. role="button" on a heading, role="presentation" stripping a real table) is explicitly OUT OF SCOPE and untested.

Programmatic-hiding scenario is exercised by only one mechanism (aria-hidden=true); no display:none, visibility:hidden, hidden attribute, off-screen positioning, or hidden-ancestor cases despite CSS Styling being a required input aspect.

All failing tokens are obvious typos/inventions (lnik, searchfield, bibliographic-reference); no abstract-role cases (e.g., role="widget", role="input", role="section") which are valid keywords but explicitly disallowed and should also fail — abstract-role rejection is in the expectation but not demonstrated.
Case-sensitivity, leading/trailing/multiple-internal whitespace normalization, and tab/newline separators within the token list are not exercised beyond the basic single-space cases.
No SVG element examples even though SVG is explicitly in the applicability scope; all targets are HTML (input, span, div, img).
No dynamically-injected or scripted role changes (role set/changed via JS, frameworks, ARIA attributes computed at runtime) — only static authored markup.

Roles drawn from Graphics-ARIA and other satellite specs are not represented among the valid examples (only core ARIA searchbox/link and DPUB doc-biblioref), so the breadth of the accepted vocabulary is under-demonstrated.
Each example is purpose-built to isolate exactly one condition; real pages stack many role attributes with mixed validity, interacting hiding, and nested landmarks, none of which appear here.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every `headers` attribute on a table cell is a valid intra-table reference: each space-separated token in the attribute must (1) be the `id` of an element that is itself a cell of the SAME `<table>` element, and (2) not be the cell's own id (no self-reference). It is a purely structural/syntactic integrity check on the explicit header-to-data-cell association mechanism (the id/headers technique, H43). It does NOT verify that the referenced cell is semantically a header, that the association is the "right" one, or that any association exists at all when omitted.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "Relationships" limb of 1.3.1 — specifically that programmatically-determined relationships (here, the data-cell-to-header-cell relationship in a data table) are correctly conveyed in the markup/accessibility tree. It targets the failure mode F90 (incorrectly associating table headers and content via headers/id), i.e. a relationship that the author asserted via `headers` but that is broken/dangling so the intended structure is not actually programmatically determinable. It does NOT touch the "Info" limb (visual semantics) nor any other 1.3.1 relationship beyond table header association.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any `headers` attribute specified on a cell within a `<table>` ELEMENT, where the table is (a) visible, (b) included in the accessibility tree, and (c) has a semantic role of table, grid, or treegrid. Note the deliberate narrowing: only real `<table>` elements count — ARIA-only grids built from `<div role="table">` are explicitly inapplicable (the `headers` attribute has no defined meaning outside native tables). Tables hidden via display:none, off-screen positioning, role="presentation", or re-roled away from table/grid/treegrid (e.g. role="heading") are all inapplicable.
ruleIntents.expectation: Two expectations, both must hold for a pass. Expectation 1: every token in the `headers` value is the id of an element that is a cell of the same table (referenced cell exists, is in THIS table, and is a th/td-type cell — including td with role=columnheader/rowheader, or even another data cell). Expectation 2: none of the tokens is the id of the cell on which the `headers` attribute itself sits (no self-reference). Outcome mapping: any fail => SC not satisfied; all pass => "needs further testing" (a pass here does NOT prove 1.3.1 is met, only that the references are not broken).

syntheticNarrowness: Every fixture is a bare 2-4 row/column toy table with placeholder text ('Projects', 'Objective', '15%') — no real data tables with many rows, financial figures, irregular spans, nested headers spanning multiple levels, or the multi-axis tables where the headers/id technique is actually NEEDED (the technique exists for complex tables, yet the cases are almost all trivial tables where scope= or implicit association would suffice).

The single FAIL mode for a broken reference is a one-character typo ('headOfColumn1' for 'headerOfColumn1'). Failed Example 2 puts the data cells in a literally separate sibling <table> with no header row content — an artificial split a human author would essentially never produce; the realistic cross-table-leak case (e.g. nested tables, or layout tables wrapping data tables) is not represented.

No fixture exercises partially-correct headers lists (e.g. a multi-token value where SOME tokens resolve and one is dangling), which is the common real failure for cells associated to several headers; coverage treats each value as wholly-right or wholly-wrong.

No dynamic / scripted scenarios: ids or headers injected/removed by JavaScript, tables rendered client-side, ARIA live regions, or sortable grids where header associations change — all collapsed away by static synthetic HTML.

Visibility/a11y-tree edge cases are only the textbook ones (display:none, position off-screen, role=presentation). Real ambiguous cases (visibility:hidden, aria-hidden=true on the table vs. on a cell, opacity:0, zero-size, off-screen-but-focusable, CSS that visually hides only specific cells) are absent.

The rule and fixtures only ever check the REFERENCE integrity; they never probe whether the association is semantically meaningful or correct (a cell could point to a valid-but-wrong header and still pass), so the test corpus gives no signal on the most common real 1.3.1 table failure: present-but-semantically-wrong header relationships.

No coverage of headers attribute on cells in scrollable/responsive tables, tables inside iframes/shadow DOM, or tables with thousands of cells where the unique-id assumption breaks at scale — i.e. nothing that stresses the assumptions the rule explicitly declares.

All fixtures are single-language English, no caption/summary, no nested tables, no <table> inside a <td>, and no mixed presentational+data table — so the 'same table element' boundary is only tested with two cleanly-separated tables, never the genuinely confusing nested-table boundary case.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks ARIA "required owned elements" containment: when a container element has a semantic role that constrains its children's roles (e.g. role=list, grid, menu, tablist, listbox, row, table, treegrid), every element it OWNS in the accessibility tree must have a role drawn from that container role's required-owned-elements list. It validates the role-of-children, not the presence/quantity of children, and recurses into nested containment chains (e.g. menu -> group -> menuitem; grid -> row -> gridcell). Owned-ness is resolved via the accessibility tree, including aria-owns and skipping elements with role=none/presentation or otherwise excluded from the a11y tree. It is purely a structural/role-conformance check, not a rendered-output or behavioral check.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "relationships" limb of SC 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) — specifically that structural relationships conveyed by a composite ARIA widget's role (the container-to-required-child pairing, e.g. a list to its listitems, a grid to its rows/cells) are programmatically determinable. It does NOT touch the "info"/text-semantics side (headings, labels, emphasis) or table data-cell/header association beyond the generic role-containment requirement.
ruleIntents.applicability: Any HTML or SVG element that (a) is included in the accessibility tree and (b) has a WAI-ARIA 1.2 semantic role (explicit or implicit) whose role definition specifies "required owned elements" — e.g. list, grid, menu, menubar, tablist, listbox, tree, treegrid, row, table, radiogroup, etc. Excluded: elements with an inclusive ancestor in the a11y tree whose aria-busy=true; elements not in the a11y tree (aria-hidden=true, hidden, display:none); and roles that have NO required owned elements (e.g. progressbar). Scope is limited to ARIA 1.2 Recommendation roles (Graphics/DPUB modules excluded).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each in-scope element owns ONLY elements whose semantic role appears in the required-owned-elements list for that element's role; nested required-owned roles that themselves carry containment requirements (arrow "containing" notation, e.g. menu's group -> menuitemradio) must satisfy them recursively. An owned element with a role outside the list (including a generic/no-role child, a link inside a list, a treeitem where listitem is required, or a group where group is no longer permitted) fails. Note: subclass roles are NOT auto-accepted (treeitem does not satisfy list's listitem requirement). The rule's assumption caveat: if the role is misapplied but the real relationship is already programmatically determinable, a rule failure may not be an actual 1.3.1 failure.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every form-field control exposed in the accessibility tree has a non-empty accessible name (after trimming whitespace). It computes the accessible name via the ARIA accname algorithm (native label association, aria-label, aria-labelledby, placeholder, wrapping label, etc.) and asserts the result is not the empty string "". It does NOT check that the name is meaningful, correct, matches a visible label, or that the control has a visible label at all — only that some non-empty name string exists.
ruleIntents.scLimb: This rule is PRIMARILY mapped to 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (the "Name" component); 1.3.1 is only a SECONDARY/related requirement per the rule's own mapping. For 1.3.1 it touches the narrowest possible slice: the programmatically-determinable label/control RELATIONSHIP for form fields — i.e., the limb where a control's identifying label must be programmatically associated with (and thus exposed for) the field. It exercises 1.3.1's "relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined" only insofar as a missing accessible name means a visually-presented label is NOT programmatically tied to its control. The rule explicitly notes 1.3.1 is STRICTER than what it tests (1.3.1 covers all info/structure/relationships, not just presence of a name).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any element included in the accessibility tree that EITHER (a) has one of the form-field semantic roles: checkbox, combobox (select), listbox, menuitemcheckbox, menuitemradio, radio, searchbox, slider, spinbutton, switch, textbox; OR (b) is an input with no semantic role and type = color, date, datetime-local, file, month, password, time, or week. Excludes elements not in the a11y tree (display:none, aria-hidden, role=none). Deliberately includes disabled fields (AT can list them) but excludes button/menuitem and option/menu/tree roles (they don't inherit from input/select).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each target element has an accessible name that is not the empty string "". Whitespace-only names (e.g. aria-label=" ") are trimmed to "" and therefore fail. Outcome mapping: any failed = SC not satisfied; all passed = needs further testing; inapplicable = needs further testing.

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that an element carrying an explicit WAI-ARIA role which has a "required context role" actually sits — in the accessibility tree, not just the DOM — directly inside an ancestor that provides that required context role. Concretely (per ARIA 1.2): a role="listitem" must be an accessibility-tree child of a list/group/feed-style context (the rule restricts to list as the required context for listitem), a role="row" inside a rowgroup/grid/table/treegrid, a role="option" inside a listbox, role="menuitem" inside a menu, etc. The structural relationship that conveys "these items belong to this container" must be programmatically present so AT can announce "list, 2 items / item 1 of 2". If the role is orphaned (no qualifying context parent in the a11y tree) the relationship is broken and SC 1.3.1 fails.
ruleIntents.scLimb: 1.3.1 "...relationships... that are presented through presentation can be programmatically determined." Specifically the RELATIONSHIPS limb (not the "info"/structure-text limb), and even more narrowly the container-to-item grouping relationship: that a child role implying membership in a collection (listitem→list, row→table, option→listbox) is programmatically tied to its required parent container via the accessibility tree. It tests the parent-child containment relationship, not headings, not labels, not reading order.
ruleIntents.applicability: Any HTML or SVG element that is (a) included in the accessibility tree, (b) carries an EXPLICIT WAI-ARIA 1.2 semantic role, (c) whose role has a "required context role" defined in ARIA 1.2 — EXCEPT when the element's explicit role equals its implicit role (e.g. <li role="listitem">). Excluded by design: DPUB roles, ARIA Graphics Module roles, roles with no required context (heading), elements not in the a11y tree (display:none, role=presentation), and elements with only an implicit role.
ruleIntents.expectation: Each applicable target must be a DIRECT CHILD in the accessibility tree of an element whose (implicit or explicit) semantic role is one of the target's required context roles. Notably strict in three ways: (1) it is the a11y tree, so presentational/role=none intermediaries are transparent, and aria-owns can relocate ownership; (2) it requires a DIRECT parent-child a11y relation (stricter than ARIA's general "owned element" notion); (3) subclass roles do NOT count as the context (e.g. feed does not satisfy listitem's required list context). The context role may be expressed explicitly (role="list") or implicitly (a <ul>).

aspects.title: Genuine data tables whose header/structure semantics are absent or stripped: all-<td> tables, and real data tables with role=presentation (F91, F92)
aspects.description: A genuine data table — content where cells are only intelligible via their row/column headers — fails to expose those relationships. Two mechanisms: (1) F91, the table presents headers visually (a bold first row, a labeled first column) but every cell is a plain <td> with no <th>, scope, headers/id, or role=columnheader/rowheader, so a screen reader announces bare values with no context; (2) F92, a structurally correct data table (or list, or heading) carries role=presentation/role=none, deliberately suppressing its semantics from the a11y tree. Both require the human judgments: is this content actually a data table whose cells need headers, and which row/column visually functions as the header? A checker sees either zero header cells (F91 -> rules inapplicable) or a deliberately suppressed tree (F92 -> excluded from scope).
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability of the data-table header-to-data relationship and of table semantics themselves (TT 14.A table identification, 14.B cell-header association); data tables must retain semantics and must not be suppressed.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT's table rules (a25f45, d0f69e) require a <th> or role=columnheader/rowheader to even be applicable — a table built entirely of <td> returns inapplicable from both, so F91 is silently out of scope. For F92, ACT treats role=presentation / aria-hidden purely as an INAPPLICABILITY trigger (element removed from a11y tree -> structural rule doesn't apply); the corpus therefore uses presentation-role only to exclude elements, never as the failure itself, and never contains a real data table marked role=presentation that should FAIL. Distinguishing 'correctly suppressed layout content' from 'wrongly suppressed data table' is the omitted human judgment.

references.quote: This failure occurs when data tables do not use header elements (th) or other appropriate table mark-up ... to make the headers programmatically determinable from within table content.
This failure occurs when a role of presentation is applied to an element whose purpose is to convey information or relationships in the content.

Verdict requires recognizing the content IS data and identifying the visual header line.

aspects.title: Layout tables that falsely assert data-table relationships: th, caption, scope, or summary on a positioning-only table (F46)
aspects.description: A table used purely to position page regions (nav | content | sidebar, or a hero/marketing layout) includes data-table semantic markup — a <th>, a <caption>, scope attributes, role=table, or a non-empty summary — which falsely tells AT that the layout grid is meaningful tabular data and that, e.g., 'Page Title' is the header for the nav/content/footer cells. The inverse of the suppression case: here genuine semantic markup is present and syntactically valid, but the relationship it asserts does not exist. Judging this requires recognizing the table is layout (no real row/column data relationship) AND that it nonetheless asserts header semantics. Automated tools see a structurally valid <th>/<caption> and pass; they cannot decide the table is 'really' layout (TT 14.C).
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic relationships must not assert structure that does not exist: a layout table must not designate itself as a table or carry header structure/attributes (TT 14.C).
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT table rules (a25f45, d0f69e) check the INTERNAL correctness of header references and that th cells have assigned cells — they assume the table IS a data table and verify the plumbing. No ACT rule asks 'is this a layout table that should not carry th/caption/summary at all?', so F46 (correct markup, wrong context) is wholly outside the corpus. The layout-vs-data distinction is precisely TT 14.C, a human determination a static checker cannot make.

aspects.title: Valid structural elements asserting relationships that do not exist: heading/blockquote/fieldset used for visual effect (F43)
aspects.description: Genuine structural elements are present and syntactically valid, but they assert a content relationship that is false. An <h3>/<h4> makes an author byline or address big and bold (no new section begins), a <blockquote> wraps text that is not a quotation merely to indent it, or a <fieldset>/<legend> draws a decorative bordered box around prose that is not a group of form controls. Automated tools see a well-formed heading/blockquote/fieldset and pass; only a human reading the content can tell the asserted relationship is untrue. This is the Trusted Tester note 'don't use heading markup for emphasis' and F43's 'relationships that do not exist in the content.' It also fabricates a misleading heading outline (e.g. every ingredient as its own <h5>).
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic relationships must reflect the actual content: structural markup must not indicate relationships (sectioning, quotation, control-grouping) that are not present in the content (TT 10.B note, F43).
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT rules check that structural elements are syntactically correct and carry required properties — never whether the relationship they assert is TRUE of the content. No fixture contains a structurally valid <h4>, <blockquote>, or <fieldset> whose correct verdict is FAIL because the element misrepresents its content. The corpus has no notion of 'valid markup, wrong meaning,' which is precisely the human semantic judgment this aspect needs.

references.quote: a failure that occurs when structural markup is used to achieve a presentational effect, but indicates relationships that do not exist in the content. This is disorienting to users who are depending on those relationships to navigate the content

aspects.title: Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)
aspects.description: A form's field-to-label, field-to-instruction, and field-to-group relationships are conveyed only by visual placement and styling, not programmatically. Examples: a label sits visually next to/above an input but is not associated (no <label for>, no aria-labelledby, no wrapping), so AT cannot tell which text describes the field; a set of radio buttons or checkboxes answers a question shown as a visual heading above them with no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=radiogroup, so the group's question is lost; required-field status or a 'pick one' cue is shown only by red text or a visually adjacent note not programmatically tied to the field. Trusted Tester 5.C asks whether the combination of accessible name, description, and OTHER programmatic associations describes each field including instructions and cues, and notes radio/checkbox groups must be associated with their question — a contextual reading-and-layout judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability of form relationships: which label/instruction/cue governs which field, and which fields form a group sharing a common question (TT 5.C; ARIA17/fieldset grouping; required-cue association).
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT form rule in scope (e086e5) only checks that a form field has a NON-EMPTY accessible name — a binary presence test a static checker already does. It does not evaluate whether the RIGHT visible label/instruction is the one associated, whether a multi-field group (radios/checkboxes answering one question) is programmatically grouped, or whether a visually-conveyed required/'choose one' cue is tied to the field. Deciding which adjacent text functions as the label, and that several controls share a visually-shown group question, is contextual human judgment outside the corpus.

references.quote: The combination of the accessible name, accessible description, and other programmatic associations (e.g., table column and/or row associations) describes each input field and includes all relevant instructions and cues (textual and graphical).
At minimum, radio buttons and checkboxes should be programmatically associated with their question and response.
Any label associated with the group also serves as a common label or qualifier for individual controls in the group.

aspects.title: Emphasis or special-status meaning conveyed only by visual text variation, with no markup or text equivalent (G117, H49)
aspects.description: Information is carried solely by a variation in text presentation — bold/italic/underline, a different font face or color, strike-through, larger size — with neither semantic markup (<strong>/<em>/<ins>/<del>) nor an equivalent stated in text. Examples: 'new' or 'on sale' items shown only by bold/red with no '(new)' word; deletions/insertions shown by strike-through/underline with no change list; a glossary term distinguished only by a different font; a warning shown only in red. WCAG explicitly excludes pure color (1.4.1), but bolding/italics/font/strike that convey status, emphasis, or special meaning fall under 1.3.1 (G117/H49): the relationship 'this text has special status' must be exposed via markup OR available in text. Judging which formatting carries meaning (vs decoration) and whether that meaning is otherwise available requires reading the content.
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability OR text-availability of information conveyed by variations in text presentation (emphasis, special status), excluding color which is 1.4.1 (G117, H49).
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT 1.3.1 rule addresses emphasis or special-status text conveyed by presentation; the corpus is entirely about ARIA properties, roles, owned/context roles, table headers, and accessible-name presence. A page where 'sale' items are bold-only, or insertions are underlined with no markup/text equivalent, has nothing for any rule to evaluate. Deciding that a font/weight/strike variation CARRIES information (not mere decoration) and that the information is not otherwise stated in text is a human content-meaning judgment. (Pure-color cases are deliberately excluded as 1.4.1.)

references.quote: When the visual appearance of text is varied to convey information, state the information explicitly in the text. Variations in the visual appearance can be made by changes in font face, font size, underline, strike through and various other text attributes.
words that have special status are indicated by changing the font family and /or bolding, italicizing, or underlining them
It is not required that color values be programmatically determined. ... Success Criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color addresses the specific case of color, rather than Success Criterion 1.3.1

Selector inaccuracy (not verdict-changing): doc names `td.cancelled, th.cancelled` and claims the styling is on `<td>/<th>`, but the CSS rule (line 42) is scoped to `td.cancelled` only. Computed styles confirm each `<th class="cancelled">` row-header (e.g. 'Wed 18 Mar', 'Mon 30 Mar') renders fontStyle:normal / textDecoration:none — it is NOT italic or struck-through. Only the three `<td>` cells per cancelled row receive the cue. The `th.cancelled` part of the selector therefore carries no styling and the date cell is visually un-marked, a minor inconsistency. Suggested fix: change CSS to `td.cancelled, th.cancelled { font-style:italic; text-decoration:line-through; }` so all four cells of the row are visually marked, matching the documented selector.
Even after the fix the page would still FAIL 1.3.1 — the cue would remain presentation-only with no text/programmatic equivalent — so the outcome label is unaffected.
